AM7-01.note: Opening-of-form literal equation. Same one learned habit as AM7-11 and AM7-19 (isolate a named variable); three items on that template.

AM7-02.note: The 2x2 sign/direction grid is the right option set for this.

AM7-03.solved: 3 km per 2 cm = 1.5 km/cm; 12 x 1.5 = 18 km.
AM7-03.note: 15 does not come from a natural wrong path; 8 (12*2/3) and 24 (12*2) do.

AM7-04.note: Exponent-law family with AM7-13, AM7-14, AM7-23 (four items).

AM7-05.note: Sign and reciprocal errors both represented.

AM7-06.note: 36 and 9 are the two natural stopping-short answers.

AM7-07.note: Clean 2x2 grid (coefficient error x constant error).

AM7-08.note: 300 = 18/0.06 and 950 = 57/0.06 are real wrong paths; 632 corresponds to nothing (39/0.06 = 650), so one option is filler.

AM7-09.solved: Times 30/12 = 2.5 h and 30/20 = 1.5 h, total 4 h for 60 miles; 60/4 = 15 mph.
AM7-09.note: The famous harmonic-mean trap, and 16 (the arithmetic mean) is the right trap option. Still ONE idea, executed correctly, so medium and not hard by this project's bar.

AM7-10.note: Rational-expression family with AM7-16 and AM7-25 (three items: factor/clear denominators).

AM7-11.note: Same template as AM7-01 and AM7-19. Options are the exact 2x2 of the two errors (dropping the 2, wrong sign on b2), which is good distractor design but makes the template even more learnable.

AM7-12.note: Two of the four options (12, 14) are EVEN and are eliminated by the stem without any work, leaving 11 vs 13; then 11*13 confirms in one multiplication. This is the weakest option set in the batch. Also note -13 and -11 have product 143 too, so the stem technically admits a second integer pair - it is only saved by that pair not being offered.

AM7-13.note: 32 (the ratio itself) and 20 (four doublings) are good; 6 is filler. Exponent family with 04/14/23.

AM7-15.note: IDENTICAL METHOD to AM7-21 (square the given sum, subtract twice the product). A student who learns one answers the other with no new thought.

AM7-16.solved: Multiply numerator and denominator by 3x: (3 + x)/(3 - x) = (x+3)/(3-x).
AM7-16.note: The sign 2x2 is exactly right here; a careless student lands on C. Rational family with 10 and 25.

AM7-17.note: 20 is the length, the right trap. Fully back-solvable from the options in under 20 seconds, which caps it at easy. Same translate-two-sentences habit as AM7-18 and AM7-20.

AM7-18.note: 7 is the pen count. Same system-of-two habit as 17 and 20; also back-solvable.

AM7-19.note: Third literal-equation item (with 01 and 11), and the third time the tested error is 'did you keep the factor of 2 in the right place'.

AM7-20.note: 23 is the larger number, 18 is half the sum. Third item on the two-sentences-to-two-equations template (17, 18, 20).

AM7-21.note: Same identity as AM7-15 with 1/x substituted for y. 27 (adding 2) and 25 (the square itself) are the correct traps, but the item adds no new idea to 15.

AM7-22.note: HARD, but the weakest of the four I graded hard. Two ideas do interact: the compound absolute-value inequality with a fractional lower bound, then a parity count that must include 0 and the negatives. 15 (all integers in range) and 4 (positive evens only) are the two errors students actually make.

AM7-23.note: Fourth exponent-law item. Routine once you write everything base 2 - a five-line computation, which by this project's bar is medium, not hard.

AM7-24.solved: Infinitely many solutions means the second equation is a multiple of the first; 6/3 = 2 so k = 5 and c = 24. k + c = 29.
AM7-24.note: One recalled condition then two divisions. 17 and 11 are filler; only 44 (k = 10 unscaled) reflects a real path.

AM7-25.solved: 2x/(x^2 - 9) = 1 -> x^2 - 2x - 9 = 0 -> product of roots = -9 (roots 1 +/- sqrt(10), neither excluded).
AM7-25.note: HARD: clearing a rational equation, recognising the result is quadratic, and then answering with Vieta rather than solving. 2 is the SUM, the right trap; 9 is the sign error. Sits in both the rational family (10, 16) and the Vieta family (15, 21, 27).

AM7-26.note: Graded medium, not hard: this is one standard mixture equation and the inequality is decorative - the boundary value IS the answer, so a student who writes '=' scores it. A genuinely hard version would make the inequality change the answer.

AM7-27.solved: Product of roots = 36, difference 5 -> 4 and 9; k = sum = 13.
AM7-27.note: HARD: Vieta's product must be combined with an integer-difference constraint, and only then does k come from the sum. Short once seen, but the two ideas genuinely interact. 37 is the (1,36) pair, 9 is a root, 20 is filler.

AM7-28.note: HARD: needs the nth-term formula AND the sum-of-n-terms formula (no ACT formula sheet), then a simultaneous solve. 9 is d, 27.5 is 165/6 read as a term. The best-constructed hard item in the batch.
